A benchmark for vision models

Jigsaw Bench

A model gets scans of a jigsaw puzzle's loose pieces and has to work out the picture they make. It never sees the box.

Why jigsaws

Jigsaws and layered visual understanding

Jigsaws are relaxing: find the next piece and see the image being revealed. But imagine you're not allowed to move any of the pieces. Then a jigsaw turns into a challenging visual processing task involving two steps:

  1. Put it together

    Work out how the pieces fit: which ones form the edges, which colours and shapes continue across a join, which way up each piece goes.

  2. Look inside the result

    Describe the assembled picture, including where everything sits relative to everything else: the barn left of the pond, the dog in front of the tractor.

Humans can't solve this task well. How well do LLMs do?

→

Looking only. No tools, no code.

Models get no code interpreter, no image editing and no web search, so they can't crop, rotate or stitch the scans. They have to do it in their head.

Models can describe the picture. They can't put it together.

What Opus built

The farmyard puzzle (54 pieces), rebuilt from Opus's answer: each piece is moved to the cell where Opus placed it. Yellow outlines mark the 12 of 54 pieces in their true place. Its neighbour score is 0.23, against 0.02 for a random arrangement.

Sky goes roughly to the top and mud to the bottom, but little else lines up.

Orientation

Portrait pictures come out sideways

Every answer states whether the picture is landscape or portrait. The models call nearly every portrait picture landscape, so their whole description is turned 90°. Opus got none of the 9 portrait cuts right.

Piece ID tags

Numbering the pieces changes nothing

For the assembly task each piece gets a random three-digit tag. We ran the description task with and without the tags on otherwise identical scans: the scores barely move. The tags only helped Haiku count the pieces.

Method

How it works

  1. Pieces in

    The model gets the scanned pages and one prompt. The pieces are never assembled for it.

  2. Answer out

    Either a description of the finished picture, ending with its orientation, grid and piece count, or the assembled grid of piece IDs.

  3. Scored

    A judge model grades descriptions against a hand-reviewed rubric and the real picture. Assemblies are checked directly against the true layout.

The puzzles

AI-generated pictures, cut with classic tab shapes, rotated at random and rendered as scans. The puzzle size is fixed, so more pieces means smaller pieces. The 8 scored pictures are each cut at about 50, 100 and 200 pieces (24 puzzles). To keep them out of training data, they're shown here only pixelated, with one small part left sharp.

The farmyard puzzle used as the example on this page is not one of them. It isn't scored, so it can be shown in full.

Scoring a description

Each picture has a rubric of 34–49 weighted items. A model drafted each rubric from the picture, then a person checked every item against the picture, correcting or removing items where needed. The judge marks each one and also checks every claim in the answer against the picture. Here is part of Opus's grade for the farmyard puzzle.

Completeness

How much of the rubric the answer got: correct earns an item's full weight, partial half.

Correctness

The share of the answer's own claims that are true. Inventing things lowers it.

f1

The harmonic mean of the two, so a model can't score well by saying little, or by saying everything.

Orientation, grid size and piece count are scored separately and don't change f1.

Scoring an assembly

The model answers with a grid of piece IDs, which is checked against the true layout without a judge. It is told the grid size. The neighbour score is the share of truly adjacent pairs that the answer puts side by side in the right order, so a correct patch still counts if it's shifted. The direct score is the share of pieces in exactly the right cell. A random arrangement scores about 1 divided by the number of pieces on both.

Caveats

  • Claude models only so far. Other vision models are next.
  • One run per puzzle. 24 puzzles per model and task, so small differences between models are within noise.
  • The judge is Opus 5.5, which is also one of the models tested.
  • Effort levels: each model ran at its default effort (shown in the legend) unless stated.
